title: Delhi Police Asks MEA to Cancel Passports of 10 Gangsters Operating from US, UK, and Canada
excerpt: The move targets fugitives linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi network, Khalistan Tiger Force, and cross-border extortion rackets — and raises questions about diaspora security
body:
The Delhi Police have formally requested the Ministry of External Affairs to cancel the passports of at least ten individuals identified as fugitive criminals and terror operatives who are believed to be sheltering in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Dubai. The move represents one of India's most aggressive efforts to neutralise criminal networks that have increasingly shifted their operations overseas.

The list includes some of the most wanted names in Indian organised crime: Himanshu Bhau, operating from the United States; Kapil Sangwan and Rohit Godara, believed to be in the United Kingdom; Arshdeep Singh Gill (known as Arsh Dalla) and Gurjant Singh, suspected to be in Canada; and Rashid Cablewala and Sachin Kumar Golu, thought to be based in Dubai.

By cancelling their Indian passports, authorities aim to strip these fugitives of their primary travel document, confining them to their current locations and making it easier to pursue extradition proceedings.

## The Bishnoi Network's Global Reach

Several of the listed individuals are connected to the Lawrence Bishnoi criminal syndicate, which has grown from a regional Rajasthan-Haryana operation into a transnational enterprise with tentacles stretching across four continents.

Rohit Godara, from Bikaner, is alleged to have connections with both the Goldy Brar and Bishnoi networks. He has been linked to the conspiracy behind the 2022 murder of Punjabi singer Sidhu Moose Wala — a crime that sent shockwaves through the global Punjabi diaspora and highlighted how Indian gang rivalries had migrated abroad.

Kapil Sangwan, who fled to the United Kingdom in 2020, is accused of murder, extortion, and land-grabbing in Delhi and Haryana. A Red Corner Notice was issued against him in 2021, yet he has remained at large, reportedly running operations remotely.

In the United States, Himanshu Bhau is believed to manage a crime network from American soil after initially fleeing to Portugal. He is wanted in connection with the Burger King murder case of June 2024 and multiple shooting incidents across Delhi, Haryana, and Punjab. Venkat Garg, also in the US, allegedly runs an extortion syndicate from Georgia, while Yogesh Kadiyan and Randeep Malik — the latter linked to the Bishnoi gang — are similarly suspected of operating from American cities.

## The Canada Question

The inclusion of Arsh Dalla on the list is particularly significant. Described by the MEA as the "de facto chief" of the banned Khalistan Tiger Force, Dalla is a proclaimed offender with more than 50 charges against him, including murder, attempted murder, and terrorism-related offences. India sought his provisional arrest in Canada in July 2023, but the request was denied — a refusal that became a flashpoint in the already strained India-Canada relationship.

Dalla's continued presence in Canada, alongside associates like Gurjant Singh who allegedly extorted ₹4 crore from a Delhi businessman and orchestrated grenade attacks in Punjab, underscores the diplomatic friction that India's pursuit of these fugitives creates.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the millions of law-abiding Indians in the US, UK, and Canada, the presence of these criminal networks in their cities is more than an abstract concern. Extortion calls targeting diaspora businesses have increased sharply in recent years, with gangsters leveraging social media to threaten shopkeepers, real estate agents, and restaurateurs in cities like Brampton, Surrey, and Birmingham.

The passport revocation strategy also raises questions about the adequacy of Western law enforcement responses. Despite Red Corner Notices, Interpol alerts, and formal diplomatic requests, many of these fugitives have operated in plain sight for years, exploiting gaps between Indian criminal proceedings and Western legal protections.

For Indian diplomatic missions, each passport cancellation creates additional work — consular staff must navigate host-country legal systems, coordinate with local law enforcement, and manage the reputational risk that comes with high-profile extradition requests.

## An Evolving Approach

The Delhi Police's request represents a shift in strategy. Rather than relying solely on extradition — a process that can take years and is frequently blocked by legal challenges — passport cancellation aims to immobilise fugitives immediately. Without a valid Indian passport, these individuals cannot travel freely, open bank accounts in many jurisdictions, or maintain the appearance of legitimacy that enables their operations.

Whether the MEA will act on all ten requests, and whether the host countries will cooperate in enforcing the cancellations, remains to be seen. But the move signals that India is escalating its pursuit of criminal networks that have used the diaspora's geographic spread as a shield.
